abstract: Placental dysfunction has been associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy which are primarily characterized by high maternal blood pressure newly diagnosed after 20 weeks of gestation (gestational hypertension). Of these, early-onset preeclampsia ([≤] 34 weeks) has dominated previous research because it is associated with more severe adverse outcomes for the mother and fetus, but late-onset preeclampsia with mild features or late-onset gestational hypertension (>34 weeks) is much more common and can be life-threatening for the mother during pregnancy and increase the risk of future health complications. As sex differences have been observed in the incidence of late-onset preeclampsia (more common when carrying a male fetus), we analyzed differential gene expression in placental tissue from full-term deliveries of ten late-onset gestationally hypertensive and ten normotensive pregnancies, each with nearly half carrying a fetus assigned female at birth (46,XX karyotype) and half assigned male at birth (46,XY karyotype). Every placenta was sampled at four evenly distributed locations, allowing analysis of intraplacental variation across the placental disc. Gene expression differences between hypertensive and normotensive pregnancies in female placentas were enriched for antigen receptor mediated signaling, response to angiotensin, cell junction disassembly, and ribosomal genes. In male placentas, gene expression differences between hypertensive and normotensive pregnancies were enriched for ribosomal genes as well as genes involved in mitochondrial function and DNA/RNA processing, immune system, and inflammatory functions. Comparisons with two previously published preeclampsia datasets identified overlapping placental gene expression signatures which included inflammatory and immune response genes in male placentas and cell adhesion and extracellular matrix organization genes in female placentas. Genes with increased intraplacental variation in gene expression in hypertensive pregnancies were enriched for muscle cell differentiation, vascular development, and response to mechanical stimulus, all related to the establishment of the feto-maternal interface. Previously reported placental marker genes of preeclampsia such as LEP and FLT1 showed greater differential expression comparing hypertensive to normotensive pregnancies in male placentas than in female placentas and were among the highest in intraplacental variation. In summary, we show that differences in placental gene expression associated with late-onset gestational hypertension vary by fetal sex.
